items.summary: I am posting some highlights from my master's thesis I thought could be interesting to this audience. items.title: Control questions matter: introspection, refusal ablation, and gates in open Gemma models

items.summary: A mechanistic interpretation for baroclinic normal mode instability with exponential growth is the interaction arising from Counter-propagating Rossby Waves (CRWs), where pairs of CRWs phase-lock and interfere constructively. On the other hand, an arbitrary initial condition can lead to finite transient growth as long as there is constructive interference. The present work investigates the characteristics of finite time transient instabilities and its description in terms of CRWs in a baroclinic system with asymmetric interaction, in contrast to usual settings where there is an inherent symmetry that leads to equal and opposite CRWs. A sloped Eady problem on a $f$-plane is considered here, which has the benefit that there are only two CRWs in the system, and the presence of a bottom topographic slope can be formulated in a such a way…
items.title: Transient growth and Counter-propagating Rossby Waves in a sloped Eady problem

items.summary: TL;DR A good understanding of where LLM no-chain of thought (no-CoT) two-hop reasoning succeeds and fails is important for monitorability as well as for designing belief instillation-based misalignment evaluations. Prior work suggests that LLMs are limited in their ability to perform no-CoT two-hop reasoning with pairs of fabricated, fine-tuned propositions. Here, I show on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3-8B that this limitation only holds if the bridge entity connecting the propositions is also fabricated or particularly obscure — models successfully compose such fabricated propositions if the bridge entity is real, and success rates vary with how well-known it is. I also demonstrate that, with real and well-known bridge entities, the source of the other entities barely matters — models achieve roughly comparable two-hop reasoning accuracies…
items.title: Small LLMs perform no-CoT two-hop reasoning on synthetic facts with real bridges

items.summary: Epicurean status: strawman, kind of. Gourmet George: Yum! This chocolate is so sweet and tasty. Sweet Caroline: Yeah, it’s pretty good. items.title: How it feels talking to a hedonistic utilitarian

items.summary: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then…
items.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs

items.summary: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They…
items.title: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability

items.summary: This paper develops skew-symmetric formulations and energy stable finite difference schemes for the reactive Euler and reactive Navier--Stokes equations. By introducing suitable transformed variables, we rewrite the governing equations into skew-symmetric forms and obtain continuous energy estimates by standard integration-by-parts arguments. The proposed formulations extend the skew-symmetric framework for compressible flow equations to reactive systems, where the chemical energy and the species equation must be incorporated into the transformed variables. Based on these formulations, we construct semi-discrete schemes with summation-by-parts (SBP) operators. The convective terms are discretized by the non-dissipative part of linear upwind SBP operators, while a nonlinear SBP--WENO operator is used only to supply artificial dissipation…
items.title: Skew-Symmetric Formulations and Energy-Stable Schemes for Compressible Reactive Flow Equations

items.summary: This is a side project from my time in the Anthropic Fellows Program. The benchmark items, prompts and scripts are in the pushback-bench repository. 1. I studied how much and when AI assistants push back on choices people have already made and ask the assistant just to execute on the decision. 2. items.summary: Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users. Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations. We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities. At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks…
items.title: Steerable Pluralistic Policy Alignment from Anonymized Crowd Feedback

items.summary: TL:DR Earlier this year I introduced the very simple Social Deduction game of Carrot-Parsnip and showed that most models are better-than-random at identifying Parsnips (the hidden, deceptive role) and that being a strong Parsnip (skilled at strategic deception) does not perfectly correlate with being a strong Carrot (skilled at deception detection). I have recently completed a substantially larger experiment with 10 models and over 5000 games. I have attempted to fit the results to a four-parameter model tracking Parsnip deception, Parsnip divisiveness, personal accuracy (as Carrot) and teammate assistance (as Carrot). I believe that my results demonstrate the potential for Carrot-Parsnip (and minimalist Social Deduction games in general) to act as the basis for a multi-agent benchmark of LLM strategic deception and deception detection…
items.title: CarrotParsnipBench: A Lightweight Multi-Agent Deception and Detection Eval

items.summary: Alignment is missing a causal account of what leads to suffering and flourishing. In this post I propose one based in psychology. I am coming from an unconventional background compared to most in this community. I was an engineer before becoming a psychotherapist. Every day I use talk therapy to help people restore function and reduce suffering. I’ve noticed that most of the alignment community has technical backgrounds in computer science, mathematics, engineering and physics. The contributors here are incredibly intelligent and capable. The gamble this post is going to make is that the problem of alignment is also a psychology problem, not just a technical one. The applications alignment utilizes are technical (training methods, interpretability tools, evaluations and benchmarks, etc.) but the principles the field is deriving those…
items.title: Alignment is Missing a Causal Account

items.summary: Pluralistic alignment aims to represent meaningful variation in human preferences rather than collapse heterogeneous judgments into a single target. Yet existing work often mixes three distinct questions: what pluralistic behavior a model should exhibit, whose preferences define the reference, and what evidence is sufficient to demonstrate success. We organize the literature around a two-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 distinguishes representing a range of human-supported viewpoints (Overton Pluralism), adapting faithfully to a specified perspective or preference condition (Steerable Pluralism), and matching the response distribution observed in a target population (Distributional Pluralism). Layer 2 distinguishes aggregate populations, countries and regions, and subgroups as human references. Preference representation, implementation…
items.title: Pluralistic Alignment in Language Models: Objectives, Human References, and Preference Representations

items.summary: Epistemic status: We found useful uncertainty signal in three reasoning models. All experiments were run on three seeds and are fully reproducible. Whether the same approach can become a broader tool for monitoring models is still an open question. Lingo might include “intend” or “conscious” and has to be taken with a grain of salt. TL;DR: We provide an uncertainty estimation method for reasoning models. Building on the J-lens, we construct four orthogonal directions in a model’s hidden-state space: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. Together, these directions span the U-space. As the model reasons, we measure how closely its hidden states align with each direction. Paired with the average entropy of the model’s next-token probability distributions across reasoning tokens, this yields the U-lens…
items.title: Uncertainty in the Verbalizable Workspace

items.summary: What would it take to get assurance that we have actually explained a neuron? Certainly, it would be a good sign if neuron activations looked like they had a consistent pattern, and a bad sign if they looked like a random jumble of unrelated concepts. Nick Cammarata’s recent post makes an important and true observation: in the past, people have been too quick to write off neurons as polysemantic, but if you look harder, there is actually often a simple pattern behind the activating examples. This historically caused people to overestimate how much polysemanticity there is. This is a really good point and we should update on it. But it’s nowhere near a sufficient argument that we understand most of what neurons are doing, and these results do not show that interpretability is solved, or even that it is vastly easier than previously…
items.title: Neural networks are not already clean
